newsitem.title: CANADA: Scotiabank sees Canadian growth leading G-7 in '97.
newsitem.headline: Scotiabank sees Canadian growth leading G-7 in '97.

text.p: Canada's economy will lead the Group of Seven (G7) nations in growth next year, powered by low interest rates and strong exports, Bank of Nova Scotia economists predicted on Thursday.
"Overall, 1997 is shaping up to be Canada's best year this decade in terms of a sustainable, broadly based economic performance," said Warren Jestin, Scotiabank's chief economist, in a statement.
Jestin forecast the economy will grow by almost 3.5 percent next year, rapidly improving government finances and ending the era of "bad news government budgets".
"Exports will remain the backbone of this country's improving economic performance," said Jestin, who noted Canada is the export growth leader among OECD nations.

Bank economists predicted Canada's merchandise trade surplus will climb to C$40 billion in 1997, helped by a strong U.S. economy, improving prosects in Europe and Latin America and rising commodity prices. These factors should also result in a current account surplus in 1997.
Broadening growth on the domestic front is also reinforcing the bank's optimism about Canada's prospects, economists said.

With mortgage rates near three decades lows, the 1996-97 revival in housing activity will mark the strongest two-year advance in residental construction in a decade, Jestin said. Retail sales also picked up sharply at the end of 1996, and stronger job and income growth should bolster consumer purchases this year, he said.

Bank economists said even with the stronger growth, Canada's inflation rate will remain below the U.S. rate for an "unprecedented" seventh year in a row. However, with the U.S. Federal Reserve likely to raise rates this year "the best of the low interest rate news is over" in Canada.
Canadian interest rates will likely follow U.S. rates higher this year while remaining below U.S. levels, the bank said.
"Canadian interest rates will remain quite low by the standards of the 1980-90s, particularly with our dollar likely to rise to a US$0.75-US$0.77 range by by year-end," said Jestin.

Regionally, Alberta is expected to lead Canada's provinces in growth in 1997. Strong energy prices should help Alberta's economy expand by more than 4.5 percent, the bank predicted. Ontario is also expected to see growth of more than 4.0 percent, helped by a strong manufacturing sector.

Both Saskatchewan and Manitoba are expected to record another year of strong growth, while growth in British Columbia is expected to lag the national average. East of Ontario, only New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are expected to experience growth of more than two percent, bank economists said.
